Dear Diary,
Unit test results today. I came second. SECOND. Avni came first by half a mark.
Everyone said "wow, 97!" but all I could hear was that I wasn't first. Our principal only reads out the topper's name in assembly. I've been topper since Class 6. I, Sonali, am the one people call "the brain".
I studied every night this month till one. I skipped Avni's birthday. I didn't even go for badminton.
When Papa asked why I was quiet at dinner, I couldn't explain. It's like I'm only worth something when I'm at the top. If I'm not first, who am I?
Tomorrow I'm going to make a timetable for the finals. Maybe with one hour of badminton in it. Maybe.

qa.a: Sonali feels crushed and disappointed, as if worth depends on being first, and cannot enjoy a score of 97.

In the small town of Sangli, the Class 10 board results were pinned outside the school gate, and Parul pushed through the crowd. She had topped the district last year and the local newspaper had printed her photo. Her uncles still showed it to guests.
Her name was fourth.
Parul's face went hot. Around her, girls were cheering. Her friend Manjula hugged her. "Parul, 94! That's amazing!"
"It's fourth," Parul said, barely audible.
Walking home past the sugar factory, she didn't speak. At home she went straight to her room and pulled out next year's books. She had not been to the river with her cousins all year. She'd told herself there would be time later.
Her mother knocked. "Come and eat. Marks are marks. You are still you."
Parul didn't answer. But she opened the door.

I, Indu, was twenty, at a women's college in Allahabad. I wanted to be general secretary. Partly because the hostel food was terrible and nobody listened. And partly, I'll be honest, because I liked the idea of people knowing my name.

Then I noticed I was deciding everything myself. I didn't consult the others. When a junior girl disagreed, I made sure she wasn't on any committee. One day my friend Vimla said, 'You've become the thing we complained about.'

"I want to fix the broken hostel water pumps and get a fair fee-refund system," she said. "And yes, I want a seat at the table where decisions happen."
Her friend Rajni watched, arms folded. Later she said, "You know what worries me? Last week you told the second-years they'd 'better vote for you if they want the new wing'. That sounded like a threat."
Alka's cheeks went hot. "I didn't mean it like that."
"Then don't say it like that."
Alka looked at her torn posters. She wanted to lead. She didn't want to become someone people feared.
